title: Hybrid vibration energy harvesting based on piezoelectric polyline beams with electret coupling
venue: Journal of Intelligent Materials Systems and Structures

sections.heading: Hybrid vibration energy harvesting based on piezoelectric polyline beams with electret coupling
sections.text: Jianan Pan $^ { 1 , 2 } _ { \textcircled { \mathbb { D } } }$ , Weiyang Qin1 , Chaoyang Zhao2 and Yaowen Yang2

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: Aiming at harvesting vibration energy more efficiently, a hybrid energy harvester is proposed, which integrates the piezoelectric and electrostatic effects. It is composed of two piezoelectric polyline beams and an electret film. The two piezoelectric polyline beams stand closely, of which one is covered by an electret film, while the other is covered by a counter-electrode. Under base excitations, the electret film interacts with the electrode, by which the two polyline beams can excite each other and form a broad frequency band of large vibration, thereby generating a large output. The dynamical equations are derived and the simulations are carried out. For validation, the experiments are conducted. The experimental results prove that the hybrid harvester is more efficient in harvesting stochastic vibration energy. For $\mathsf { P S D } = 0 . 0 0 4 | \ g ^ { 2 } / \mathsf { H z } ,$ , the two piezoelectric polyline beams can generate the power outputs of 47.9 and $2 3 . 6 ~ \mu \mathsf { W } ,$ respectively.

sections.heading: Keywords
sections.text: Energy harvesting, stochastic excitation, electret coupling, piezoelectric material

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Harvesting renewable energy in the environment and transforming it into electronic power are promising for powering wireless sensors and actuators. In this field, vibration-based energy harvesters developed rapidly and can be categorized into five modes: the piezoelectric energy harvesters (Kim et al., 2018), the electrostatic energy harvesters (Feng et al., 2018), the electromagnetic energy harvesters (Fan et al., 2019), the piezoelectric-triboelectric energy harvester (Li et al., 2018), and the piezoelectric-electromagnetic energy harvester (Toyabur et al., 2018). The piezoelectric energy harvesting converts vibration energy into electric energy employing the piezoelectric effect. It has attracted much interest in recent years due to its advantages of low cost, simple design, and good portability. On the other hand, the electret-based energy harvester works based on the electrostatic effect. Under external excitations, the system’s oscillation will lead to a variation in capacity, creating a charge rearrangement, and thus generating a charge flow in the external circuit.

Many kinds of piezoelectric energy harvesters have been proposed and reported (Eltanany et al., 2017; Izadgoshasb et al., 2019; Upadrashta and Yang, 2016; Xu and Tang, 2017). Friswell et al. (2012) proposed a nonlinear energy harvester with a vertical cantilever beam and a tip mass. Numerical and experimental results indicated that the pre-buckled beam could give a high output power with a broadened bandwidth. Borowiec et al. also studied the buckled beam under vertical excitation. They showed that the increased tip mass and stochastic excitation intensity could produce a double-well vibration and generate large power output (Bilgen et al., 2015). Garg and Dwivedy (2019) carried out a vertical cantilever beam’s dynamic analysis with a tuned mass. This tuned mass position was optimized to realize a 3:1 internal resonance, which could achieve a broader bandwidth than the linear one. To further enhance the performance, a multiple degree-of-freedom (DOF) structure consisted of an L-shaped beam and magnets was investigated by Chen et al. They demonstrated that in the magnetically tunable L-shaped design, the internal resonance could be induced and significantly improved the working bandwidth (Chen et al., 2016). Xiong et al. (2018) designed a comprehensive 2-DOF system consisting of two cantilevers. The experimental results indicated that the operational bandwidth was extended dramatically.

![](images/7388a1e49e1cfba6db1517fc44607bb1d78d3fd0aa9c2bcf4668fc4e3928e5af.jpg)  
Figure 1. Schematic of proposed hybrid energy harvester and lumped model for electrostatic part: (a) schematic and (b) equivalent model.

The electrostatic energy harvesters (EEHs) can be classified into two types. One is the in-plane EEH, in which the overlap area between two electrodes changes with time (Peano and Tambosso, 2005; Wang and Hansen, 2013); the other is the out-of-plane EEH, in which the gap between two electrodes changes with time (Asanuma et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2019). In general, the vibration direction in the in-plane EEHs is parallel to the electrode surface, whereas in the out-of-plane EEHs is normal to the electrode surface. Because of their advantage of low production cost, the out-of-plane EEHs have been extensively studied, focusing on their fabrication and improvement in efficiency. Boisseau et al. (2011) proposed a cantilever electret energy harvester and carried out the design optimization. The optimization analysis of the air gap, the load resistance, and the electret length showed that the proposed system was efficient in harvesting lowfrequency vibration energy. Ghavami et al. (2018) presented an electret-based energy harvester composed of a cantilever and a substrate. It was found that the resistance had a significant damping effect on the dynamic responses of the system. Gao et al. (2017) proposed a vibration energy harvester based on a double-ended beam electret. The capacitance variation brought by design could give a high output and achieve wide bandwidth. Tao et al. (2018) proposed a multimodal electret energy harvester with an impact mechanism. The simulation and validation experimental results revealed that the nonlinearity induced by impact could produce a wider bandwidth. Yang et al. (2019) presented a broadband electret energy harvester, which could realize a high output for the low frequency and low-level excitations.

In this work, we propose a hybrid energy harvester composed of two piezoelectric polyline beams, an electret layer and a counter-electrode. The simulation and experiments demonstrate that the hybrid energy harvester can achieve high output. The rest of the article is organized as follows. In Section 2, the hybrid energy harvester’s governing equations are derived by the Lagrange equation, while the electrostatic field is introduced by employing Kirchoff’s law. In Section 3, the polyline piezoelectric beams with electret coupling are modeled in Simulink, and the numerical simulations are carried out. In Section 4, a prototype of the proposed hybrid harvester is fabricated, and the validation experiments are conducted with both frequency sweep and stochastic excitations. Finally, a few concluding remarks are summarized in Section 5.

sections.heading: 2. Hybrid piezoelectric and electrostatic energy harvester
sections.text:
The schematic of the proposed hybrid piezoelectric and electret energy harvester (HPEEH) is illustrated in Figure 1. The system consists of two polyline beams (PB I and PB II), of which the inverted beams are the primary parts, while the inclined short beams are the auxiliary parts. A piezoelectric patch of macro-fiber composite (MFC) is bonded to the root of each inverted beam. An electret layer is covered on PB II and a counter-electrode on PB I. The electrostatic part of the HPEEH is composed of the electret and counter-electrode. The electret is charged by the localized corona charging method in advance. When the HPEEH is excited by a base motion, the inverted beams will oscillate, which changes the distance between the electret and the counter-electrode. The electrical power will then be generated from the capacitance variation between the electret and the counter-electrode. On the other hand, to obtain a wide working bandwidth, the two beams are designed to be slightly different in their natural frequencies by adjusting the weight of each polyline beam’s tip mass. As for the external excitation, the system is supposed to be excited by a base motion in the vertical direction. The dynamical model of HPEEH is shown in Figure 2. sections.heading: 3. Model verification and numerical simulations
sections.text:
In this part, based on the governing equations of equations (9) and (11), the corresponding simulations are carried out. To reveal the dynamical characteristics of HPEEH, the frequency sweeping excitation is applied to obtain its amplitude-frequency response. By adjusting the tip mass, one can get the desired distribution of two polyline beams’ resonance frequencies. The two polyline beams’ resonance frequencies should be designed to be staggered to achieve a wide working frequency band. In practice, the weights of tip mass of polyline beam I are chosen to be $\mathbf { M } _ { 1 } = 0 . 0 1 6 \mathrm { k g }$ and $\mathbf { M } _ { 2 } = 0 . 0 3 1 ~ \mathrm { k g }$ , which yields $f _ { 1 } = 6 . 9 7 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ and $f _ { 2 } = 1 5 . 3 1 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ ; and those of polyline beam II are $\mathbf { M } _ { 3 } = 0 . 0 2 3 ~ \mathrm { k g }$ and $\mathbf { M } _ { 4 } = 0 . 0 4 3 ~ \mathrm { k g }$ , which yields $f _ { 1 } = 5 . 9 1 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ and $f _ { 2 } = 1 2 . 8 2 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . The resonance frequencies $f _ { 1 }$ and $f _ { 2 }$ correspond to the first two modes of HPEEH. To further illustrate the modes, the FEM model is established, and the simulation results are illustrated in Figure 3. The two modes result in different motions. The first mode could produce a large displacement, which may lead to the impact between the two inverted beams. Then, the auxiliary inclined beam vibrates more intensely in the second mode than in the first mode. The parameters used in the equations and experiments are listed in Tables 1 and 2.

![](images/5d3b36def8957b5475181704712fad98ef9651ef21d673132b917088d0d2f82e.jpg)  
Figure 3. Modes of HPEEH: (a) the first order and (b) the second order.

To obtain the frequency response of output voltage of HPEEH and validate the results obtained, the numerical simulations are performed based on the derived equations and the frequency sweeping excitation is applied, where the excitation magnitude is set varying from $a _ { \mathrm { z } } = 0 . 1 \ \mathrm { g }$ to $a _ { \mathrm { z } } = 0 . 2 ~ \mathrm { g }$ , with $R _ { \mathrm { p } } = 6 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . The output voltage across MFC is shown in Figure 4. The frequency responses of PB I and $\mathrm { I I }$ exhibit a linear manner under weak excitation, that is, the polyline beams vibrate separately without interaction. When the excitation varies from $a _ { \mathrm { z } } ~ = ~ 0 . 4 3$ g to $a _ { \mathrm { z } } = 0 . 5 3 ~ \mathrm { g } .$ , as shown in Figures 5 and 6, the two beams are engaged and the responses exhibit nonlinear behavior. The impact in this work is induced by the intense head-on motion between the two polyline beams. The impact position is located at the top ends of the primary inverted beams. Since the coefficient of restitution of the impact depends on the materials involved, and the polyline beam is made of stainless steel, the coefficient $e$ will be in the range of 0.63–0.93. Finally, we make a comparison between the proposed harvester and the inverted beam with a conventional stopper, the working frequency band of the proposed harvester is from 5.9 to $8 . 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , while that of the inverted beam-based harvester is from 6.9 to $7 . 3 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . As is clear from Figure 4, the experimental results are in good accordance with the simulation ones.

sections.heading: 4. Validation experiments
sections.text:
The experimental setup and the prototype of HPEEH are shown in Figure 7. The piezoelectric material MFC is bonded to the root of each inverted beam. The electret layer is placed on one polyline beam and the counter-electrode on the other. The HPEEH is mounted on a shaker (APS 0077, APS Dynamics), which is controlled by a vibration controller (VR9500, Vibration Research) and a power amplifier (APS 125, APS Dynamics). The output voltages across the electret layer and MFC are recorded by a data acquisition module (NI 9229, National Instruments). ![](images/94d81037c45e7a87e2832acf3025167fb9e81b41a118b96a7050a59d0bcb868b.jpg) Figure 4. Output voltages of MFC of polyline beams I and II at first resonance with $R _ { p } = 6 0 0 ~ \mathsf { k } \Omega$ : (a and c) experimental results and (b and d) simulation results. ![](images/e0ea9ed44fcc4c4998b1a8cf2295f506314d8531c185a594342948c4653509df.jpg) Figure 5. Output voltages of MFC of polyline beams I and II at impact stage with $R _ { p } = 6 0 0 ~ \mathsf { k } \Omega :$ : (a) experimental results and (b) simulation results. ![](images/4e781a26a8a798ba2ae7f0eece00ac2346315c90afcd4c382b3de94f69423eec.jpg) Figure 6. Output voltages of electret of polyline beams I and II at impact stage with $R _ { \mathrm { e } } = 1 ~ { \mathsf { M } } \Omega .$ : (a) experimental results and (b) simulation results. ![](images/9fcf79a7fbb2ef170cfbc4637ce99452b40ca719c6765d00d56381a9358fb418.jpg) Figure 7. Experimental setups and prototype of HPEEH. ![](images/9593d77755a515464ebced82dda94a27f9f9b7114ed54bf036c1acc00780a586.jpg) Figure 8. Output voltage of the electret layer under various excitation intensities with $R _ { \mathrm { e } } = 1 ~ \mathsf { M } \Omega$ . The responses are demonstrated for $a _ { \mathrm { z } } = 0 . 4 3 , 0 . 4 8$ , and $0 . 5 3 ~ \mathrm { g }$ . The voltage across the electret layer is measured as the electrostatic output, as shown in Figure 8. It is clear from Figure 8 that over the frequency range of $4 { - } 2 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , there are four voltage peaks, corresponding to the resonance frequencies of polyline beams I and II. This suggests that there exists a strong interaction between the two polyline beams, by which the HPEEH could have a broad working bandwidth. Moreover, the output voltage increases with the excitation. The maximum voltage obtained is $5 7 . 4 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ at $a _ { \mathrm { z } } = 0 . 5 3 ~ \mathrm { g } .$ , a considerably high output. The first mode motion usually leads to changes in the gap distance between the electret and counter-electrode, so the electret takes a great effect in the area of the first resonance frequency. The outputs of MFC for sweeping excitation are shown in Figure 9. As can be seen from Figure 9, the first primary resonance peak of PB I exhibits a complicated nonlinear characteristic due to the electret coupling. To show the coupling effect clearly, the HPEEH is excited at the resonance frequencies, with the magnitude of $a _ { \mathrm { z } } = 0 . 4 8 \ \mathrm { g }$ . The corresponding experimental results are illustrated in Figures 10 and 11. It can be seen that the MFC of polyline beam II gives a high output when the excitation is at its first resonance frequency of $f = 5 . 2 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ . It should be noted that owing to the interactive motion, the output of polyline beam I is considerably large as well. This phenomenon occurs again at the first resonance frequency of polyline beam I, $f = 6 . 6 5 \ : \mathrm { H z }$ , where there is notable output from polyline beam II. The results of the electret output support this observation. As shown in Figure 11, both outputs of electret at $f = 5 . 2 5$ and $6 . 6 5 \ \mathrm { H z }$ are quite large, indicating a strong interaction between the two polyline beams at these frequencies. The related parameter analysis and optimal resistance analysis are then performed and demonstrated in Figure 12. First, to investigate the influence of gap distance, we carried out the experiments for different gap distances under the harmonic excitation of $a _ { \mathrm { z } } = 0 . 4 8 \ \mathrm { g }$ and $R _ { \mathrm { e } } = 1 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ . As shown in Figure 12(a), with $g _ { 0 }$ varying at 4.65, 2.30, and $0 . 6 9 \ \mathrm { m m }$ , the output voltage increases monotonically, suggesting that the small gap is beneficial for the coupling effect. On the other hand, to find the optimal resistance for output power, the external resistance is varied from $R _ { \mathrm { p } } = 3 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $R _ { \mathrm { p } } = 1 \mathrm { M } \Omega$ . The experimental results of output power and RMS voltage are illustrated in Figure 12(b). It can be seen that the optimal resistance is $R _ { \mathrm { p } } = 6 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . With this resistance, we carried out the experiments for stochastic excitations. A brief comparison for outputs under the sinusoidal excitation is made between the piezoelectric harvesters, electrostatic harvesters, and proposed hybrid harvesters, the results are illustrated in Table 3. The hybrid harvester, which is composed of two piezoelectric polyline beams, achieves a significant output power. Moreover, the electrostatic interaction also could give an output power, although it is relatively small due to the low resonance frequencies. ![](images/d235847c0f57e7259a26c7fd928175bfeead88c64a114d69fe1beeebad6d396a.jpg) Figure 9. Experimental stochastic responses of PB I and PB II at different excitations with $R _ { p } = 6 0 0 ~ \mathsf { k } \Omega .$ : (a and b) $\mathsf { P S D } = 0 . 0 0 2 4 \ \bar { g } ^ { 2 } / \mathsf { H z } ,$ , (c and d) $\mathsf { P S D } = 0 . 0 0 3 3 ~ \mathsf { g } ^ { 2 } / \mathsf { H } \mathsf { z } ,$ , and (e and f) $\mathsf { P S D } = 0 . 0 0 4 | \ g ^ { 2 } / \mathsf { H z }$ . In the experiment, to examine the energy harvesting efficiency of HPEEH, the stochastic base excitations are realized by a shaker. The excitation is a bandlimited white noise with a frequency band of $5 { \mathrm { - } } 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ . The excitation is varied from $\mathrm { P S D } = 0 . 0 0 2 4$ to $0 . 0 0 4 1 ~ \mathrm { g } ^ { 2 } / \mathrm { H z }$ . Corresponding responses are obtained and illustrated in Figure 13. At $\mathrm { \bar { P S D } } = 0 . 0 0 2 4 ~ \mathrm { g ^ { 2 } / H z }$ , the piezoelectric outputs are relatively small, and the RMS voltages of PB I and PB II are 4.22 and $2 . 9 8 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , respectively (as shown in Figure 13(a) and (b)). Then, when the intensity is increased to $\mathrm { P S D } { = } 0 . 0 0 3 3 ~ \mathrm { g } ^ { 2 } / \mathrm { H z }$ , some high pulses of voltage appear in the response (as shown in Figure 13(c) and (d)), the RMS voltages of PB I and PB II are 5.24 and $3 . 5 7 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , respectively. Finally, at $\mathrm { P S D } = 0 . 0 0 4 1 ~ \mathrm { g } ^ { 2 } / \mathrm { H z }$ , the pulses of voltage become dense in the output. The maximum voltage of PB I could reach $2 3 . 2 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , while that of PB II is $1 7 . 6 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ (as shown in Figure 13(e) and (f)) and their RMS voltages are 5.56 and $4 . 0 1 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ , respectively. The output voltages of the electret layer under stochastic excitation are shown in Figure 14, with $R _ { \mathrm { e } } = 1 ~ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ . It is evident that the electret layer’s output is small compared to that of MFC, as the system is excited by stochastic excitations. In fact, the electrostatic part would be more efficient when the response is confined to a specific frequency. Furthermore, with the optimal resistance $R _ { \mathrm { p } } = 6 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , the output powers of PB I and II versus PSD are obtained and illustrated in Figure 15. It can be found that at $\mathrm { P S D } = 0 . 0 0 4 1 ~ \mathrm { g ^ { 2 } / H z }$ , PB I and PB II’s output powers could reach 47.9 and $2 3 . 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ , respectively. Since the stochastic excitation is more practicable, the output obtained under stochastic excitation is an objective standard for evaluating the harvester’s performance. ![](images/2e6eb8f442b6b8e9e0147c0020bbfe26fc69a1e0dbaea5e609c5eb67329543b4.jpg) Figure 14. sections.heading: 5. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this work, we proposed a hybrid piezoelectric and electret energy harvester (HPEEH), in which two piezoelectric polyline beams were clamped vertically to face each other closely, and a couple of electret and electrode was placed on the polyline beams. The governing equations were derived and simulations were carried out. The experiments were conducted to verify the simulation results and investigate the efficiency of HPEEH. From the results, the following conclusions can be drawn.

1) By adjusting the polyline beam parameters such as tip mass values, the staggered resonance frequencies can be achieved in the proposed

![](images/7f4217b9bc1c94aef71cffc9ef5795f6813b2db70af2de5ba216c445687d3f89.jpg)  
Figure 15. Experimental output powers of PB I and II versus excitation intensity with $R _ { p } = 6 0 0 ~ \mathsf { k } \Omega$ .

HPEEH. With the coupling between two polyline beams, the HPEEH could achieve a broad frequency range of large vibrations.

2) Under external excitations, both the MFC patches and the electret could generate large output through the electrostatic coupling. With the decrease of distance between the two polyline beams, the electret output will enhance considerably.

3) For stochastic excitations, both polyline beams of the HPEEH could generate large output voltages and powers, indicating that the coupling between the two polyline beams could significantly improve the harvesting efficiency.
